newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bank of Israel vows to support currency band.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Israel vows to support currency band.

text.p: Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel on Monday rejected calls for an administrative devaluation and said the central bank had the resources to support the exchange rate "as long as necessary".

"The Bank of Israel now sterilises through auctioning and bank deposits, and here we will just continue to do it as long as necessary," Frenkel said at a news conference to release the central bank's annual report.
The Bank of Israel has been buying dollars almost daily in a bid to prevent the currency basket to which the Israeli shekel is officially linked from falling below the bottom end of its trading band.

Frenkel said he saw indications that the shekel was beginning a period of real depreciation, but warned that a major improvement in the exchange rate requires the government to take measures to keep the deficit in target.
"According to what research shows it appears we are beginning a process of a real depreciation," Frenkel said, citing reduce demand by Israelis for foreign currency loans.

"This of course will depend on implementing policies themselves....It is critically important to keep on the matter of the budget deficit to the deficit reduction law and to the inflation target that the government set," he said.

The government is committed to a deficit of 2.8 percent of gross domestic product this year, although Treasury officials concede they have exceeded the ceiling in the first quarter. Inflation is targeted at seven to 10 percent.
Frenkel said it was also important for the government to move forward with structural changes, especially in ending foreign currency controls.
"I would recommend that the government adapt as a strategic goal...to make the Israeli shekel fully convertible in world currency markets," he said.
Frenkel said this should be pursued by a programme of rapid foreign currency liberalisation. Currency controls, he said, must be lowered in stages but at a faster pace than to date.

"While today the attitude that everything is forbidden except if it's permitted -- even if the permitted list grows from year to year -- the time has arrived to turn it around and say that everything is allowed except it is specifically prohibited," Frenkel said.
He noted that with Israeli foreign currency reserves at record levels of nearly $14 billion, the government had the leeway to liberalise forex rules.
